title: Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can estimate the difficulty of assessment items using only item content and metadata, rather than requiring time-consuming field testing with students. The authors frame item difficulty estimation as a practical problem in educational assessment, especially for K-5 mathematics and reading items where calibration is needed for adaptive testing and item development.

The study evaluates two GPT-4o-based approaches on 5,170 vertically scaled K-5 math and reading items from Edmentum’s Exact Path Diagnostic. In the first approach, GPT-4o directly predicts a difficulty rating for each item in a zero-shot prompt and those estimates are then aligned to Rasch difficulty values. In the second approach, GPT-4o is used to extract cognitively and linguistically grounded features, which are then entered into random forest and gradient boosting models alongside item metadata. The authors compare both approaches against grade-level dummy regressors, TF-IDF baselines, and metadata-only models.

The findings suggest that direct LLM judgments can moderately approximate item difficulty, but performance is uneven across grades and is weaker for some early-grade items. The feature-based pipeline performs better overall, especially for reading, and generally outperforms the non-AI baselines. The paper concludes that LLMs may help streamline item development and pre-screening, but structured feature extraction is more effective than asking the model for a single holistic difficulty judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT family large language model used for zero-shot analysis, feature extraction, and text generation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4o to estimate the difficulty of K-5 math and reading assessment items directly from item content and to extract structured item features for downstream predictive models.

findings.finding_summary: Using direct GPT-based estimation, the model predicted Rasch item difficulty for K-5 math and reading items better than a grade-specific dummy regressor overall. For math, holdout performance was RMSE=0.91 and MAE=0.72 versus benchmarks of 1.01 and 0.81, with r=.83 across grades; for reading, RMSE=0.86 and MAE=0.69 versus 1.04 and 0.84, with r=.81.
findings.measure: Holdout-set item difficulty prediction error and Pearson correlation against Rasch-calibrated difficulty

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single observational model-evaluation study using precalibrated assessment items, not an experimental design with student outcomes. Evidence is useful but limited to correlational prediction of item difficulty.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported correlations are strong and error reductions are modest but meaningful versus baselines, especially on reading and upper grades. However, the outcome is item-difficulty estimation rather than direct instructional impact.
